newsitem.title: INDIA: Famed India criminal plans autobiographical film.
newsitem.headline: Famed India criminal plans autobiographical film.

text.p: Notorious criminal Charles Sobhraj said on Wednesday that he wants to turn to social work when he leaves a maximum-security Indian jail and could work on a multi-million dollar movie based on his life.
Sobhraj, speaking outside New Delhi's Tis Hazari court, also said he was writing his life story which would serve as the script for a movie being negotiated.

"The contract is that I am getting an advance plus royalties," Sobhraj told Asian News International television. "They have a group of financiers who are putting $15 million to $20 million dollars to make the movie."
He is being held at New Delhi's Tihar jail where he has spent more than two decades behind bars.

Sobhraj, a French citizen born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother, was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewelry shop in 1971. Sobhraj, then 26, jumped bail before his trial could be held.

The suave, multilingual criminal was first convicted in 1978 of robbing and murdering a French tourist by slipping drugs into his chicken curry before stealing his travellers' cheques. He was acquitted 20 months later.
In another case in 1978, he was convicted of drugging and robbing a group of French tourists near India's Taj Mahal monument, for which he served a five-year prison term.
Since then, Sobhraj has been in and out of Indian jails on charges of murder, drug-peddling and robbery, often chained in iron fetters and in solitary confinement.
A judge sentenced him to life imprisonment in 1982 for poisoning an Israeli tourist to death. He was acquitted in 1983.
Two books and a film have been made about Sobhraj.

He shot to fame in 1986 when he fled from New Delhi's Tihar jail, where he was in detention pending an extradition request from Thailand to face charges of murder and attempted murder. He was captured 24 days later.
In November 1995, Thai police said he could not be extradited to stand trial in that country because a 20-year statute of limitations had expired.

Last week, a Delhi judge ordered him freed on bail from prison but his release was held up, according to his lawyers, because the Indian government had failed to inform prison authorities that the Thai extradition warrant had lapsed.
He remains charged in the 1986 jailbreak case.

At Wednesday's bail hearing, the judge granted him permission to call the producer of the film and left the courtroom, escorted by a half dozen policemen. He then put through a call from a public phone to the unnamed producer.
Sobhraj told reporters he was a reformed person who had converted to Buddhism and would like to lead a peaceful life once out of jail.
"I want to devote my life to some social work now," Sobhraj told the Press Trust of India.
Chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar said on Wednesday that he would rule on Sobhraj's bail plea at a later date.
